title: Design a food delivery platform
statement:
Design the backend of a food delivery app like DoorDash or Deliveroo. Customers browse nearby restaurants and menus, place and pay for orders, and follow their courier on a map. Restaurants accept and prepare orders; couriers receive delivery offers and share their location while delivering.

Clarify or state any other requirements and assumptions you need, then walk through your design.
facts: 20 million orders per day in 500 cities; the lunch and dinner peaks are 5 times the average.
1 million active couriers each send a location update every 5 seconds while on shift.
A customer must never be charged for an order the restaurant never receives.

keyPoints.text: splits the system into parts with clear ownership: restaurants and menus, orders, payments, dispatch and courier location
models an order as a state machine (placed, accepted, preparing, picked up, delivered, cancelled) owned by the order service
keeps payment and order consistent: authorise with an idempotency key, create the order, capture later, or void when the order fails
ingests about 200,000 courier location updates per second into an in-memory geo index or a stream, not the main database
matches orders to nearby couriers with a geospatial lookup (geohash or similar) and sends offers with timeouts and reassignment
serves restaurant and menu browsing from caches or a search index by location, because it is read-heavy
publishes order events (placed, accepted, picked up) on a queue so notifications, dispatch and analytics react asynchronously
plans for the peaks with autoscaled stateless services and data partitioned by city or region
pushes live tracking to customers over WebSockets or similar at a reduced update rate

probes.RELIABILITY: A customer's payment succeeds but the order service crashes before saving the order. What happens to the customer's money?
probes.SCALABILITY: Order traffic increases 100x during a nationwide promotion. What breaks first, and what do you change?
probes.DATA_MODEL: Which data would you keep in SQL, and which in NoSQL or in-memory stores? Why each choice?
probes.CACHING: Where would you introduce caching for restaurant browsing, and how do you handle a restaurant that suddenly closes or runs out of a dish?
probes.FAILURE_HANDLING: The payment provider is down for ten minutes at dinner time. What do customers experience?
probes.MESSAGING: How do the restaurant, the courier and the customer all learn that an order changed state?
probes.AVAILABILITY: The primary database of one region fails. How do orders in that region keep flowing?
probes.OBSERVABILITY: How would you detect that orders in one city are stuck in 'accepted' and never get picked up?
